title: Text Justification
description: Brute force to optimized: distributing extra spaces one at a time versus computing the exact base spacing and remainder directly.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given an array of words and a target width maxWidth, format the text so that each line has exactly maxWidth characters, packing as many words as possible per line and distributing extra spaces as evenly as possible between words. The last line is left justified with only single spaces, padded with trailing spaces on the right.

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Given an array of words and a target width maxWidth, format the text so that each line has exactly maxWidth characters, packing as many words as possible per line and distributing extra spaces as evenly as possible between words. The last line is left justified with only single spaces, padded with trailing spaces on the right.

blocks.title: Analogy: Justifying a Newspaper Column
blocks.text: Like a printed newspaper column where every line, except the very last one, is stretched so both its left and right edges line up perfectly, achieved by spreading extra gaps as evenly as possible between the words.

blocks.caption: Pack as many words as fit, then stretch the line to exactly the target width

blocks.text: Edge case: a single very long word that alone fills an entire line

If a single word exactly fills a line with no room for another word, that line simply contains that one word, left justified with no interior gaps to stretch, since there is nowhere to distribute extra spaces.
5. How Should We Think?
It helps to ask whether distributing extra spaces really requires placing them one at a time, and which cases genuinely need to be treated differently from each other.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The brute force correctly packs words greedily onto each line, but then distributes the needed extra spaces by literally placing them one at a time in a round robin loop across the gaps.

Observation 2: Distributing a fixed total number of spaces as evenly as possible across a fixed number of gaps, with any leftover going to the leftmost gaps, is exactly what integer division and its remainder already compute directly, with no need to place spaces one at a time.

Observation 3: The genuine complexity in this problem is not algorithmic at all, it is correctly separating three distinct cases: a normal fully justified line (needing the even space distribution), a line with only a single word (left justified, padded on the right, since there is no gap at all to stretch), and the very last line (always simple single spacing, left justified, padded on the right, regardless of word count).

Observation 4: Tracing the words "This", "is", "an" against maxWidth equal to 16 confirms the direct arithmetic approach, 8 total letters, 8 spaces needed across 2 gaps, base 4 with 0 remainder, producing "This" plus 4 spaces plus "is" plus 4 spaces plus "an", exactly matching the greedy loop's result but computed directly instead of space by space.

Recognizing that even space distribution is a single division and remainder calculation, and that the real challenge is correctly separating the normal, single word, and last line cases, is what turns a tedious simulation into a clean, direct implementation.
6. Brute Force Solution

Greedily pack as many words as fit onto each line first, then distribute the needed extra spaces between the words one single space at a time, round robin, cycling through the gaps repeatedly until every needed space has been placed.
Step by step algorithm

items: Greedily add words to the current line until the next word would not fit within maxWidth.
Compute how many total extra spaces need to be added beyond the single spaces already between words.
Add those extra spaces one at a time, cycling through each gap in turn, until none remain.

codes.python:
def full_justify(words, max_width):
    lines = []
    i = 0
    n = len(words)
    while i < n:
        line_words = [words[i]]
        length = len(words[i])
        i += 1
        while i < n and length + 1 + len(words[i]) <= max_width:
            line_words.append(words[i])
            length += 1 + len(words[i])
            i += 1
        if i == n or len(line_words) == 1:
            line = ' '.join(line_words)
            line += ' ' * (max_width - len(line))
        else:
            gaps = len(line_words) - 1
            gap_spaces = [1] * gaps                                 # start with the single mandatory space per gap
            remaining = max_width - sum(len(w) for w in line_words) - gaps
            gap_index = 0
            while remaining > 0:                                     # add one more space at a time, cycling through gaps
                gap_spaces[gap_index] += 1
                remaining -= 1
                gap_index = (gap_index + 1) % gaps
            line = line_words[0]
            for idx in range(gaps):
                line += ' ' * gap_spaces[idx] + line_words[idx + 1]
        lines.append(line)
    return lines


if __name__ == "__main__":
    words = ["This", "is", "an", "example", "of", "text", "justification."]
    max_width = 16
    for line in full_justify(words, max_width):
        print(repr(line))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Words are added to the current line greedily as long as the next word, plus its separating space, still fits within maxWidth.
Starting every gap with its single mandatory space before adding extras ensures a valid minimum layout exists before any distribution begins.
Cycling through gaps one extra space at a time guarantees the extras land as evenly as possible, with earlier gaps receiving any leftover first.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Packing words greedily and distributing extra spaces evenly, with any remainder going to the leftmost gaps first, correctly produces a fully justified line.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n plus total characters), since every character of every word and every space is written exactly once.
Space: O(total characters), for the resulting lines.

Limitation: computing the exact space distribution using a step by step loop that places spaces one at a time is more operations than necessary, when the exact base count and remainder can be computed directly with a single division and modulo operation.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: placing extra spaces one at a time and cycling through gaps repeats a small computation many more times than necessary to reach a result that is fully determined up front.

What direct arithmetic fixes: the total spaces needed and the number of gaps are both known the instant a line's words are chosen, so integer division gives the base spaces per gap immediately.

What the remainder handles: whatever total spaces do not divide evenly are exactly the leftover count, and giving one extra space each to that many leftmost gaps distributes them as evenly as the problem requires.

The core idea: compute the base and remainder directly with division and modulo, then build the line in a single pass, no space by space placement needed.

Once the words for a line are chosen, compute the total number of spaces needed and the number of gaps between words directly. Divide the total spaces evenly across the gaps using integer division to get a base amount per gap, and use the remainder to determine exactly how many of the leftmost gaps get one additional extra space. This computes the exact space count for every gap in constant time, rather than placing spaces one at a time in a loop.
9. Optimized Solution
Compute the base spacing and the remainder directly with division and modulo, then build each line in one pass.
Dry run for line words ["This", "is", "an"], maxWidth = 16

blocks.caption: Optimized: compute the exact base spacing and remainder directly, no space-by-space loop needed

codes.python:
def full_justify(words, max_width):
    lines = []
    i = 0
    n = len(words)
    while i < n:
        line_words = [words[i]]
        length = len(words[i])
        i += 1
        while i < n and length + 1 + len(words[i]) <= max_width:
            line_words.append(words[i])
            length += 1 + len(words[i])
            i += 1

        if i == n or len(line_words) == 1:
            line = ' '.join(line_words)
            line += ' ' * (max_width - len(line))
        else:
            total_letters = sum(len(w) for w in line_words)
            total_spaces = max_width - total_letters
            gaps = len(line_words) - 1
            base, extra = divmod(total_spaces, gaps)                # exact spacing computed directly
            parts = []
            for idx, word in enumerate(line_words[:-1]):
                spaces = base + (1 if idx < extra else 0)              # leftmost gaps get the extra space first
                parts.append(word + ' ' * spaces)
            parts.append(line_words[-1])
            line = ''.join(parts)
        lines.append(line)
    return lines


if __name__ == "__main__":
    words = ["This", "is", "an", "example", "of", "text", "justification."]
    max_width = 16
    for line in full_justify(words, max_width):
        print(repr(line))

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because integer division of the total needed spaces by the number of gaps gives the largest amount every gap can receive equally, and the remainder is exactly how many gaps must receive one additional space to account for the total precisely, so assigning that remainder to the leftmost gaps first reproduces the same distribution the space by space loop would have produced, just computed directly.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

This problem is mostly a careful simulation exercise, and the main skill it tests is correctly handling the three distinct cases (a normal full line, the last line, and a line with only a single word) rather than any deep algorithmic trick.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting the special case of a line with only one word, which should be left justified and padded on the right, since there is no gap between words to stretch.
Forgetting that the last line is always left justified with single spaces and padded on the right, never fully justified like the other lines.
Miscounting the total line length by forgetting to include the single mandatory space between each pair of words when deciding whether the next word still fits.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A single word longer than or equal to maxWidth","Occupies its own line by itself."],["The very last line","Always uses simple single spacing and right padding regardless of how many words it contains."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Work through the three cases (multi word line, single word line, last line) explicitly and separately before writing any code, since conflating them is the most common source of bugs in this problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid placing spaces one at a time", think: compute the base spacing and remainder directly with integer division and modulo.
If the interviewer says "what about a line with only one word", think: left justify it and pad on the right, since there is no gap at all to stretch.
If the interviewer says "what about the very last line", think: always simple single spacing, left justified, padded on the right, regardless of word count.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why does giving the remainder of spaces to the leftmost gaps first correctly reproduce the same result as placing spaces one at a time?
Why must the last line be treated differently from every other line, even if it happens to have multiple words?
How would you adapt this approach to center justify each line instead of fully justifying it?
How would this approach change if words could contain punctuation that should never be separated from the word before it?
How would you compute the total number of lines produced without actually constructing every line's text?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Reverse Words in a String, whose careful handling of multiple distinct spacing cases (leading, trailing, and interior spaces) is a related discipline of not conflating different formatting rules.

Palindrome Partitioning and other problems requiring several genuinely different cases to be handled explicitly, where the real difficulty lies in correct case separation rather than a single unifying trick.
Any problem asking to distribute a fixed total evenly across a fixed number of positions, where integer division and its remainder directly compute the answer without an iterative distribution loop.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n plus total characters) time, O(total characters) space. Optimized: O(n plus total characters) time, O(total characters) space, with direct arithmetic instead of per-space iteration for distributing gaps.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: greedy line packing followed by direct arithmetic (integer division and remainder) to distribute spaces evenly.

Core Idea: even space distribution across gaps is a single division and remainder calculation, and the real difficulty in this problem is correctly separating the normal, single word, and last line cases rather than any algorithmic trick.
Time: O(n plus total characters) for both approaches.
Space: O(total characters) for both approaches.
Most Important Observation: a problem that looks like careful simulation usually is exactly that, so correctness comes from clean case separation, not from finding a hidden algorithmic shortcut.
Interview Difficulty: the greedy packing is straightforward; correctly and separately handling the last line and single word line cases is where most implementations go wrong.
One line memory trick: divide the spaces evenly with divmod, give the leftmost gaps the remainder, and never forget the last line is different.
